title: Why We Built Artos: Capturing the Nuance in Drug Development
summary: Artos co-founder Josh Kim on why drug development needs AI that creates data, not just documents, and where the life sciences AI platform is headed.
body_markdown:
When I used to design clinical trials, a lot of the work was an argument. We’d spend weeks with the study team going back and forth on what to measure and how to capture it, and eventually everyone agreed and all of that got boiled down to a few fields in an EDC.


We never felt the loss right away. It would show up on the next study. We would be setting things up and wouldn’t remember why we had handled something a certain way last time, so we would do it the same way because it worked. Then a regulator would ask a question and we’d remember why we’d done it that way. We had captured all the data we could, but certain information just couldn’t be captured that neatly.


I was always fascinated by this feature of information in drug development. Nuance matters more here than almost anywhere else, but there has never been a good way to capture it.


By the time ChatGPT came along, I had been chewing on this problem for several years in academia, training NLP models on drug development and EHR data. And what I saw in this new class of AI was the ability to capture nuance at scale.


That was how Artos began.


## How Varun and I founded Artos


Varun Patel and I founded Artos after spending our entire careers in this space. We have collectively written thousands of pages of regulatory submissions and clinical trial documentation by hand for pharmaceutical products, medical devices, and health insurers.


I’d done it for marketing submissions at Ignyta, which Roche went on to acquire, for first-in-human trial applications at Erasca, where I’d been part of the run from founding to IPO in three years, and at the University of Chicago, where I’d gotten to sit on the site side of clinical trials. Varun had done the same work at UnitedHealthcare, at Eysz, and as a founder of Adiona, which built monitoring tools for Alzheimer’s.


Both of us had built a unique appreciation for the complexity of the unstructured data in this space. Not only had we done the work by hand, but, by training, Varun was a molecular engineer with a focus on large-scale data storage for biological data, and I had a background in AI and statistics research.


This shaped a lot of our thinking about what Artos should be. There were going to be plenty of people who would tackle different aspects of this problem; it was too big to ignore. But we would be the ones who deeply understood both the complexity of the data and the technology that works with it, and who could build a platform that did the work life sciences teams needed.


This was the core of Artos’s identity then, and it’s still the core now. Every person on[our team](https://artosai.com/about) is a scientist and a technologist: our engineers have no excuse not to understand how to determine a NOAEL, and our scientists have no excuse not to understand how our agent harnesses facilitate search over large datasets. Ultimately, we believe that this is what builds something really valuable in the life sciences.


## Why is unstructured data a problem in drug development?


Pharma is not short on data. It is one of the most data-rich industries out there. The problem is the shape of the data.


Some of it has been structured for a long time: trial results in clinical databases, safety cases in safety systems, assay and sequence data in discovery tools. But the reasoning around that data lives in natural language. Why a dose was chosen, how a finding was interpreted, what was said to a regulator and why: all of it sits in protocols, study reports, summaries, meeting notes, and email. For decades there has been no good way to use any of it at scale.


And it’s not for lack of trying. At the end of the day, science is complicated and it moves quickly. It’s very difficult to come up with a predefined structure that neatly captures all of the data that exists now and might exist in the future in all the ways you may need to use it.


The natural default, therefore, tends to be toward the lowest common denominator. In some cases, that means that you have some meaningful structure to your data. In many cases though, that means that you default to a document or a PowerPoint.


As a result, a very large amount of work in the life sciences is related to 1) producing these assets in a way that captures the specific nuance around the asset, and 2) following processes around how to share and manage these assets. Much less work focuses on how to use those assets more systematically.


## What does Artos do?


Artos is the[life sciences AI platform](https://artosai.com/platform) that creates data, not just documents. It supports the work teams do with unstructured data in the life sciences: creating documents, collaborating on them, governing them, updating them, and more. It’s a platform that is designed to capture all the nuance in this free-form content as data you can build on, so each piece of work builds on everything before it.


Right now, 24+ teams ranging from 10-person biotech teams to 50,000-person organizations rely on Artos to accomplish[mission-critical tasks](https://artosai.com/who-its-for) including drafting regulatory documents, responding to health authority queries (HAQs), amending protocols, ensuring consistency across a range of related documents, and identifying safety risks, all[with controls that support GxP, 21 CFR Part 11, other standards regulators require](https://artosai.com/security) , and the strict governance that comes with highly sensitive data.


We’ve taken particular care to build a system that can be deployed at scale. As great as LLMs are, the complexity of life sciences work means that this isn’t a given. We think very carefully about how end-user experience interacts with process enforcement in our products, how configurability relates to ease of use, where full automation is acceptable and where a human-in-the-loop is important. At the end of the day, building a great product in this space is more of an art than a science, and I’m incredibly grateful to our team and our partners in industry for how far they’ve advanced what is possible.


## What’s next for Artos?


While everything I’ve described is about dealing with work associated with unstructured data, the real benefit of what we’re doing is that we’re creating a way to organize this unstructured data more robustly while allowing people to do the work they need to do today. And when you can find a way to build robust structure around data, incredible things happen.


This fundamental characteristic of information is what made[AlphaFold](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03819-2) possible, and what allowed scientists to identify the[rheumatoid arthritis drug baricitinib](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(20)30304-4) as a drug that eventually treated patients hospitalized with COVID-19.


And our mission at Artos is to bring that characteristic of information, that structure, to the volumes of unstructured data that exist in drug development right now to make the next scientific breakthroughs possible.
